newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Creditanstalt suitors to decide on improved bids.
newsitem.headline: Creditanstalt suitors to decide on improved bids.

text.p: The two main bidders for Austrian privatisation candidate Creditanstalt will decide next week whether they may top up their original bids for the country's number two bank, Austrian news agency APA said on Friday.

Austrian Finance Minister Viktor Klima, in charge of the sale which has been dragged into its seventh year amid growing political controversy, last week said he would give bidders until January 10 to improve their existing offers.

The agency quoted sources inside Bank Austria, which has bid 16.8 billion schillings ($1.5 billion) for the government's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt, as saying the bank would decide on January 9 whether it may offer additional sweeteners.
A rival consortium of bidders led by insurer EA-Generali was reported to have scheduled a meeting for January 8.

The group has bid a total of 13.8 billion schillings for the state's 19.9 million shares in the bank and wants to sell about a quarter of those on the market at a premium, 60 percent of which would also go to the government's coffers.

"We're not prepared to pay an unjustified premium," a member of the consortium was quoted as saying. "If we top up our offer, then only if we are prepared to make a contribution to the improvement of the banking sector."

Bank Austria's bid is preferred by Austria's dominant Social Democrats, while their junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, prefers the consortium. The debate has caused a growing rift among the partners.

Details of a third offer by former Austrian retail king Karl Wlaschek have not been made public. Domestic media have speculated Wlaschek may team up with one of the two other bidders, but the notoriously reclusive 79-year old has not commented on those rumours.

The government's advisor in the sale, investment bank JP Morgan, last year valued the entire government's stake at some 18 billion schillings, including a five billion schilling premium for control of the bank.
According to current market prices, the stake is worth some 14.5 billion schillings. -- Knut Engelmann, Vienna newsroom +431 53112 274 ($ = 10.86 Austrian Schillings)
